title: Applying QNLP to sentiment analysis in finance
abstract_summary: This preprint evaluates two Quantum Natural Language Processing approaches—DisCoCat and Quantum-Enhanced LSTM (QLSTM)—for financial sentiment analysis. Using a novel ChatGPT-based method to generate realistic datasets of about 1000 sentences, the authors find that QLSTMs can be trained substantially faster and achieve near-classical performance in simulation, while DisCoCat is hampered by heavy circuit-simulation costs and delivers limited accuracy under the employed setup.
methodology_description: The authors compare two quantum natural language processing (QNLP) approaches (Quantum-Enhanced LSTM, QLSTM, and DisCoCat) on a synthetic financial sentiment-analysis task and use a classical LSTM as baseline. They generate two sentence datasets ("low" and "moderate" complexity, ~1000 sentences each) using ChatGPT prompts constrained to financial topics and labeled {negative=0, neutral=1, positive=2}. For DisCoCat they require grammatical parses and therefore substitute a pregroup parser with a CCG parser (BobCatParser from the lambeq library) to produce DisCoCat diagrams, which are then translated to quantum circuits: single-qubit word embeddings use an Euler parameterization (Rx-Rz-Rx) and multi-qubit words use d-layer IQP-style ansätze (initial Hadamards then parameterized controlled-Rz chains). Because the available DisCoCat implementation only supported CPU-based circuit simulation, they restricted DisCoCat experiments to binary classification (dropped neutral class) so the sentence meaning qubit |s⟩ could be a single qubit. For QLSTM they replace the classical LSTM cell with the QLSTM cell architecture from prior work: three-qubit one-hot encoding for the output y_t, concatenation of hidden and input vectors to form internal states h and c, and QNNs inside the gates built using the original QLSTM ansatz (data input layer with Hadamards and data rotations, a variational layer with cyclic CNOTs). Hyperparameter choices from tuning: for low complexity datasets the classical LSTM used embedding size 5, one unidirectional LSTM layer, FC hidden size 8 and no dropout; for moderate complexity embedding size 10, FC 16 and dropout 0.1. QLSTM used four qubits and one ansatz layer per QNN. Training used an 80/10/10 train/validation/test split and binary cross-entropy loss (binary for DisCoCat, multiclass for LSTM/QLSTM experiments). Training curves, loss and accuracy were reported; wallclock simulation times (DisCoCat: ~82 hours for 100 epochs on CPU; QLSTM moderate setup: simulation ~10 hours) and signs of barren plateaus with increased ansatz depth were discussed.
experimental_setup: Two ChatGPT-generated datasets (~1000 sentences each) of financial sentiment sentences (low and moderate complexity). Training/validation/test split 80/10/10. Classical LSTM baseline (embedding+LSTM+FC). QLSTM with quantum neural networks inside gates (4 qubits per QNN, one ansatz layer, 3-qubit one-hot output encoding). DisCoCat pipeline used CCG parsing via lambeq, single-qubit Euler embeddings for 1-qubit words and IQP-style embeddings for d>1 qubit words. Loss: binary cross-entropy. DisCoCat restricted to binary labels due to CPU-only circuit simulator.
dataset_used: Synthetic financial sentiment datasets generated with ChatGPT: two datasets ("low" and "moderate" complexity) of roughly 1000 sentences each, labeled negative/neutral/positive. Low complexity: mean word count ~4.9, vocab ~913, class distribution negative 34% / neutral 18% / positive 48%. Moderate complexity: mean word count ~18.4, vocab ~1608, class distribution negative 37% / neutral 17% / positive 46%. For DisCoCat experiments the neutral class was dropped (binary).

experiment_input.source: ChatGPT-generated synthetic sentences (prompted to produce financial statements labeled 0/1/2)
experiment_input.size: Approximately 1000 sentences per dataset (two datasets: low and moderate complexity)
experiment_input.labels: Negative=0, Neutral=1, Positive=2 (neutral class dropped for DisCoCat binary experiments)
experiment_input.preprocessing: No external corpora; sentences parsed with a CCG parser (BobCatParser via lambeq) to obtain syntactic types/diagrams for DisCoCat; tokenization and one-hot/embedding layers used for LSTM/QLSTM; sentence length constrained in generation (simple queries used max five words for simple set, more detailed prompt for moderate set).

experiment_process: 1) Data generation via ChatGPT prompts to create labeled financial sentiment sentences. 2) Preprocess and parse sentences: for DisCoCat convert parses (via CCG/BobCatParser) into DisCoCat diagrams; for LSTM/QLSTM use token embeddings. 3) DisCoCat: map words to parameterized quantum states (single-qubit Euler or multi-qubit IQP layers), translate diagrams to circuits, postselect measurement of auxiliary wires to extract sentence qubit (binary task), train variational parameters via gradient-based optimization over multiple epochs. 4) QLSTM: build sequence model replacing classical gate networks with QNNs inside LSTM gates (QLSTM cell); encode inputs, propagate hidden and cell states, output via 3-qubit one-hot encoding; QNN ansatz per gate (data input layer + variational layer with cyclic CNOTs); train parameters over epochs with backpropagation. 5) Classical LSTM baseline: embedding layer, unidirectional LSTM, FC hidden layer, dropout, ReLU activations, trained similarly. 6) Evaluation: report training/validation loss and accuracy curves; compare wallclock training times. Training used binary cross-entropy (binary for DisCoCat, multiclass for LSTM/QLSTM) and typical epoch-based optimization (epochs up to 100 in experiments).
experiment_output: Reported metrics: training and validation loss and accuracy curves. Baseline classical LSTM and QLSTM reached >80% validation accuracy on the low-complexity dataset within ~20 epochs; on moderate complexity QLSTM required ~100 epochs before progress and showed training time increases (simulation ~10 hours). DisCoCat (low complexity, binary) showed only marginal improvement over random guessing (~50% accuracy) after 100 epochs and required ~82 wallclock hours on CPU. Results included qualitative comparisons of convergence speed, final accuracy, and simulation runtimes as primary outputs.

experiment_parameters.loss_function: Binary cross-entropy (binary experiments); multiclass cross-entropy implied for 3-class LSTM/QLSTM

QLSTM_parameters.hidden_cell_shape: Concatenation of previous hidden state and input vector

hardware_details: DisCoCat experiments used a CPU-only circuit simulator (the available DisCoCat software referenced on the authors' GitHub only supported CPU simulation); the (Q)LSTM implementation had GPU-support available (used for some experiments) but specific GPU model/provider not specified. Moderate-complexity QLSTM simulation on small cloud compute took ~10 hours; DisCoCat 100 epochs took ~82 hours on the CPU simulator. No quantum hardware (QPU) was used.
reproducibility_notes: The authors reference a GitHub repository for the DisCoCat implementation (https://github.com/ichrist97/qnlp_finance) and used the public lambeq library (BobCatParser). The datasets were generated with ChatGPT prompts but the paper does not provide a public download link for the generated datasets. The DisCoCat implementation they used is CPU-only and therefore subject to runtime constraints; full reproducibility may require access to the same code, lambeq versions, and the generated datasets or the exact ChatGPT prompts. Overall reproducibility is partial: code references are provided but the generated data and exact training configuration details (optimizer, learning rates, shots) are not fully specified.

results_summary: The paper presents a comparative case study applying two QNLP approaches—Quantum-Enhanced LSTM (QLSTM) and DisCoCat—to financial sentiment analysis on synthetic datasets (~1,000+ sentences generated via ChatGPT). Empirically, QLSTMs trained much faster and reached validation accuracies comparable to a classical LSTM baseline on a low-complexity dataset within ~20 epochs, whereas the DisCoCat implementation (CPU-simulated, binary task) required very long wallclock times (100 epochs ≈ 82 hours) and yielded accuracy close to random. On a moderate-complexity dataset QLSTMs needed many more epochs (~100) before improvement, suggesting optimization challenges potentially linked to barren plateaus. The authors emphasize software/hardware simulation limitations (notably lack of GPU support for their DisCoCat implementation) and propose that improved implementations could materially change DisCoCat results.

Experimental results show QLSTMs can match classical performance in their simulation setup (not surpass), while DisCoCat performance was hampered by simulation/software bottlenecks; authors treat any advantage as possible but unproven and contingent on better implementations/hardware.

key_ideas: #idea:quantum-advantage — QLSTM models in simulation reached near-classical performance (e.g., >80% validation accuracy on the low-complexity set) and trained substantially faster in this setup compared to the DisCoCat pipeline, suggesting a possible training-time benefit for certain QNN-based sequence models.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — The QLSTM experiments used very small NISQ-style circuits (4 qubits per QNN, one ansatz layer) and thus demonstrate feasibility of small-scale QNLP experiments for financial sentiment tasks; by contrast DisCoCat proved impractical under CPU-based simulation and required simplifications (binary task) to run.

#idea:hybrid-approach — The workflow is hybrid quantum-classical: parameterised quantum circuits (QNNs) are trained with classical optimizers inside LSTM gates, showing a practical hybrid training pipeline for QNLP in finance.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Use of ChatGPT-generated, constrained synthetic datasets (~1000 sentences) enabled controlled experiments but limits external validity and underscores the need for realistic corpora when assessing practical advantages.
contradictions: #contradiction:classical-vs-quantum — The study finds QLSTM only achieves near-classical performance and DisCoCat performs worse than a classical baseline in the tested setups, which contradicts any broad claims that QNLP models will straightforwardly outperform classical methods on financial sentiment tasks.

#contradiction:scalability — Authors report heavy simulation costs (DisCoCat ~82 wallclock hours on CPU for 100 epochs) and evidence of barren plateaus as ansatz depth increases, contradicting optimistic claims about easy scalability of these QNLP approaches to larger, practical financial datasets.
